query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase high‐entropy alloy, service‐related conditions (such as high strain rates and low temperatures) can induce local short‐range chemical ordering (SRO) at defect intersections (e.g., grain boundaries and dislocation pileups), which in turn reduces dislocation mobility and promotes brittle crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy with a random solid-solution microstructure and favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled stress treatment at cryogenic temperatures to promote SRO formation versus a thermal annealing treatment designed to minimize SRO, keeping the overall complex composition intact.
generation.conditions: High strain rate loading and low operating temperatures where dynamic SRO can nucleate under service-like mechanical stress.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale domains of short‐range order forming at grain boundaries and within dislocation intersections.
generation.mechanism: Under severe mechanical loading at low temperatures, atoms in the alloy locally rearrange into short-range ordered clusters. These clusters decrease dislocation mobility and localize stress, which favors crack initiation and brittle fracture, distinct from conventional grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples experiencing stress conditions that favor SRO will exhibit lower fracture toughness and more brittle fracture characteristics compared to samples pre-annealed to suppress SRO formation.
generation.baseline: The untreated, initially homogeneous single-phase alloy that demonstrates desirable toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to become operative under high strain rate and cryogenic conditions; under moderate service conditions, SRO formation may be minimal, and the alloy retains ductile behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical stress/temperature thresholds and the quantitative contribution of SRO volume fractions to embrittlement remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject Set A to high strain rate mechanical testing at cryogenic temperatures to promote SRO formation, and treat Set B with a pre-annealing process intended to reduce SRO. After testing, characterize the microstructure (using high-resolution TEM or atom probe tomography) to detect SRO and measure fracture toughness and crack propagation characteristics.
measurements: Microstructural analysis for SRO presence (via TEM/APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens tested under cryogenic, high strain rate conditions (Set A) do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness, or if SRO features are not more pronounced in these specimens compared to the annealed controls (Set B), then the hypothesis that stress-induced SRO formation drives brittle behavior in these alloys will be falsified.
